routes.description: Establish the anti-realist burden by denying that realism enjoys a defensible common-sense, historical, or semantic presumption and by showing that a substantive anti-realist alternative survives the principal conceptual objections raised against it.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the alleged realist advantages depend on unreliable attribution, contested semantic assumptions, or projection of specialist categories, while anti-realism remains a coherent position with consequences distinguishable from rival relativist accounts.

motionBridge.description: Show that common-sense, historical, and semantic considerations do not establish a presumptive advantage for moral realism over anti-realism.

centralBridges.description: Establish that ordinary or remembered pre-philosophical outlooks cannot reliably be classified using determinate contemporary metaethical categories.
Show that historical convergence claims must overcome projection, translation, source-selection, cultural-contact, and specialist-competence problems.
Articulate a genuinely metaethical anti-realist alternative whose semantic and practical commitments remain distinct from agent-relative obligation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify what surveys, linguistic use, memory, and behavior can establish about moral thought without treating them as direct tests of moral reality.
Show that interpretive or epistemic mediation does not uniquely discredit anti-realist positions when comparable access problems arise elsewhere.

routes.description: Establish the realist burden by defending common-sense or historical evidence for an objective conception of value and by showing that the proposed anti-realist distinctions do not defeat the resulting realist presumption.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if suitably competent pre-philosophical or cross-era sources provide credible evidence of objective-value commitments and if the anti-realist alternative either collapses into a perspectival variant or fails to displace that evidential presumption.

motionBridge.description: Show that common-sense, historical, or semantic evidence supplies moral realism with a meaningful presumptive advantage over anti-realism.

centralBridges.description: Identify a defensible common-sense evidential population despite the limitations of unreflective street-level surveys and raw response variation.
Establish that sufficiently comparable philosophical or intellectual traditions converge on objectively intended value claims despite substantive disagreement.
Show that agent and appraiser relativism share an underlying perspectival structure sufficient to limit the claimed semantic or metaphysical contrast.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for heterogeneous reports through competence, motivation, ignorance, or other factors that need not undermine an initial realist seeming.
Explain how an agent's interpretation of external standards bears on the claimed practical separation between relativist positions.

sections.title: Empirical Semantics and Metaphysical Scope
sections.rationale: The parties must delimit what evidence about linguistic use, psychology, surveys, or behavior can establish about ordinary meaning and whether any such finding bears directly on moral reality.

sections.title: Common Sense and Pre-Theoretical Outlooks
sections.rationale: A claimed common-sense advantage depends on identifying competent evidence of pre-theoretical commitments and resolving whether memory, reflection, pragmatic effects, and response variation permit reliable attribution.

sections.title: Historical Convergence and Metaethical Attribution
sections.rationale: The historical branch of the motion turns on whether cross-era intellectual traditions provide comparable evidence of objective-value commitments despite projection, translation, source-selection, and cultural-independence concerns.

sections.title: Agent and Appraiser Relativism
sections.rationale: The conceptual viability of the anti-realist alternative depends on whether these forms of relativism differ in semantic, metaphysical, and normative structure or merely redescribe one perspectival position.

sections.title: Normative Conflict and Epistemic Mediation
sections.rationale: Conflicting standards and first-person interpretation test the practical implications of the relativist distinction and whether access limitations create a distinctive problem for anti-realism.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: An empirical metaethical methodology is unstable if it relies on ordinary speakers as evidence about moral language while treating those speakers as confused about the concepts under investigation.
moves.attributionBasis: The surrounding exchange identifies Derek as the questioner addressing Lance directly and presenting the methodological challenge.

response.rationale: This constructive methodological challenge supplies an initial reason to question selective reliance on ordinary speakers; it has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly frames a material methodological tension but leaves the alleged inconsistency somewhat compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The methodological objection is recoverable, though the kinds of reliance and confusion that would create instability are not fully delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It is presented as a probing methodological concern rather than a demonstrated contradiction, fitting the limited support in the span.

charity.alternative: Empirical evidence may concern language use without treating speakers as reliable metaethical theorists.
charity.decisiveQualification: The challenge remains only if the methodology actually transfers authority between those distinct evidential roles.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is intelligible, but it needs the bridge that evidence about usage commits the investigator to speakers' conceptual competence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The span states the alleged methodological practice but supplies little specific evidence that the two attitudes are combined inconsistently.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally challenges how common-sense evidence can support the realist route, although it does not itself establish realism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly identifies a possible tension, but the strongest role-differentiated methodology substantially narrows its reach.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies empirical psychological research using ordinary self-reports and raises the alleged tension concerning speaker confusion.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Empirical inquiry can establish what non-philosophers think or mean, but it cannot directly determine whether stance-independent moral facts exist.
moves.attributionBasis: Lance answers Derek's explicit methodological question and develops the distinction continuously until Derek acknowledges it.

components.text: Whether empirical inquiry is being used to determine language and thought or to determine stance-independent moral reality.

response.rationale: The reply expressly separates empirically accessible claims about speakers from the metaphysical existence claim, diagnosing why the alleged methodological instability does not follow.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts and defeats the decisive inference by distinguishing the two evidential questions on which the challenge trades.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reply clearly distinguishes non-philosophers' thought or meaning from the existence of stance-independent moral facts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical limit applies specifically to direct empirical determination of stance-independent facts and is expressly scoped.

charity.alternative: The original challenge may concern reliance on confused speakers even only as evidence of linguistic meaning.
charity.decisiveQualification: Evidence about usage need not credit speakers with reliable theoretical analysis of that usage.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction is explicit and blocks the alleged inconsistency without depending on a substantial unstated inferential bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual scope distinction is well explained, though the excerpt does not independently defend a complete empirical methodology.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary empirical-calibration bridge by specifying what empirical inquiry can and cannot establish.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the strongest methodological concern while providing the decisive distinction between usage evidence and metaphysical evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly contrasts questions about stance-independent facts with directly empirical questions about what non-philosophers think.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: If realism cannot claim to represent ordinary common sense, it loses a presumptive burden-of-proof advantage rather than direct evidence for its metaphysics.
moves.attributionBasis: The response follows Derek's question about what realism would lose by abandoning cognitivist and semantic commitments.

components.text: What dialectical consequence follows if ordinary-speaker evidence cannot straightforwardly support a realist common-sense claim.

response.rationale: The move contacts the broader methodological challenge by specifying the limited consequence: loss of a common-sense presumption, not empirical disproof of realism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly explains the burden consequence, though it does not independently resolve every issue about ordinary-speaker competence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition sharply distinguishes a presumptive dialectical advantage from direct evidence against realist metaphysics.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted consequence is limited to burden allocation and is supported by the identified common-sense-default argument.

charity.alternative: Realism might have independent arguments even if it lacks a common-sense default.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move claims only loss of one presumptive advantage, not loss of every realist justification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If a common-sense presumption is unavailable, loss of that particular burden advantage follows without implying realism is false.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies the relevant presumptive argument and literature, though the prevalence and force of that argument remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly states how failure of common-sense attribution defeats the motion-level claim of a presumptive realist advantage.

representationalCharity.rationale: It expressly preserves independent realist evidence and confines its conclusion to the dialectical value of common-sense attribution.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes the common-sense default as a major realist dialectical advantage and distinguishes that advantage from metaphysical proof.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: Common-sense evidence for realism may be drawn from philosophers' remembered pre-philosophical outlooks rather than from wholly unreflective respondents unfamiliar with metaethical issues.
moves.attributionBasis: Derek explicitly develops a proposed alternative category and asks whether it has been recognized in the philosophical literature.

components.text: Whether a defensible population can still ground a realist common-sense presumption despite problems with unreflective respondents.
Whether empirical inquiry may identify what an informed pre-philosophical population previously believed.

response.rationale: The reply proposes remembered pre-philosophical outlooks of philosophers as the relevant population, directly attempting to preserve the challenged common-sense presumption.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive population problem and offers a concrete replacement, but does not yet establish that retrospective reports are reliable.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed population is clear, but 'pre-philosophical common sense' remains partly unstable between remembered belief and informed competence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker proposes a possible evidential category rather than asserting that retrospective reports conclusively establish realism.

charity.alternative: Remembered pre-philosophical outlooks may be reconstructed after philosophical training.
charity.decisiveQualification: The proposal needs evidence that retrospective reports preserve rather than recreate earlier commitments.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The population proposal is coherent, but the bridge from later philosophical competence to reliable memory of earlier views is materially undeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The proposal relies on hypothetical retrospective surveys and an example without support for memory validity or representativeness.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the indispensable realist task of identifying a defensible common-sense evidential population.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move proposes a fair alternative population but does not address the strongest reliability qualification attached to that evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt proposes surveying philosophers about their views before studying philosophy and labels this population pre-philosophical common sense.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: Variation in reported moral outlooks may reflect incompetence, motivated ignorance, or other human complexities, so street-level surveys need not defeat an individual's initial realist seeming.
moves.attributionBasis: Derek takes the floor after Lance's methodological discussion and develops several explanations for variance before stating the limited evidential consequence.

components.text: Whether heterogeneous ordinary reports necessarily remove the evidential force of an individual's initial realist seeming.
Whether survey variation has a determinate interpretation without accounting for competence and motivation.

response.rationale: The reply directly offers incompetence, motivated ignorance, and human complexity as rival explanations of variation, limiting what heterogeneous reports establish.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the inferential significance of variation, but the proposed rival explanations are possibilities rather than comparatively supported accounts.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited conclusion is recoverable, though competence and motivated ignorance are used broadly without operational criteria.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents alternative explanations as possibilities that block a decisive inference, matching the speculative support offered.

charity.alternative: Variation may genuinely reflect diverse metaethical outlooks rather than ignorance or motivational distortion.
charity.decisiveQualification: Merely possible rival explanations do not establish which explanation best fits the observed distribution.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Possible alternative explanations can defeat a necessary inference from variation, but cannot by themselves positively vindicate realist seemings.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Incompetence and willful ignorance are asserted speculatively without representative evidence, base rates, or comparison with genuine variation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary realist bridge requiring alternative explanations of heterogeneous reports.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges complexity but gives the strongest genuine-variation account no comparative evidential treatment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes willful ignorance, motivational conflict, and human complexity to explain variance in reported moral outlooks.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: A pre-theoretical stance on a theoretical metaethical question may be conceptually unstable, and retrospective reports are unreliable because memory can reconstruct or confabulate earlier commitments.
moves.attributionBasis: Lance states his own position, develops the memory objection, and then adds structural problems with open-ended and forced-choice surveys.

components.text: Whether philosophers' retrospective reports can reliably identify determinate pre-philosophical metaethical commitments.
Whether reports and response variation can be straightforwardly interpreted as evidence of stable earlier commitments.

response.rationale: The reply expressly identifies conceptual instability and reconstructive memory as reasons the proposed retrospective population cannot satisfy its evidential purpose.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly attacks both the conceptual status of a pre-theoretical metaethical stance and the reliability of retrospective access.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conceptual and epistemic objections are separately recoverable and explicitly limited to retrospective theoretical attribution.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Memory research supports substantial caution, though describing retrospective attribution as broadly unreliable slightly outruns the excerpt's detail.

charity.alternative: Carefully designed retrospective questioning might recover broad earlier tendencies despite imperfect episodic memory.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such tendencies still may not amount to determinate commitments in contemporary metaethical categories.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The two independent objections are clearly distinguished and each bears directly on the proposed evidential population.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Memory research is specifically invoked, but no study or conditions distinguishing reliable from unreliable recall are developed in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the anti-realist burden of showing that remembered pre-philosophical outlooks resist determinate classification.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply handles the strongest improved-survey alternative because its independent conceptual objection remains applicable.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls a pre-theoretical answer to a theoretical question conceptually problematic and invokes reconstructive, unreliable memory.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Empirical investigation of moral language presupposes a contestable language-as-use account of meaning rather than a purely external account of linguistic patterns.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained first-person discussion of the dissertation's empirical and metaphilosophical commitments matches Lance Bush's established position.

components.text: What account of linguistic meaning licenses treating observable speech patterns as evidence about moral meaning.
Whether speakers' internal theoretical self-understanding is required for empirical study of language use.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the methodological challenge by locating empirical language research within a contestable use-based theory rather than assuming raw reports transparently reveal concepts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It identifies the key methodological presupposition, though it does not fully defend that semantic theory against externalist alternatives.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast between language-as-use and external pattern accounts is clear, though the boundary between those descriptions remains compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents method dependence as a philosophical commitment rather than claiming that empirical work uniquely proves the use theory.

charity.alternative: External linguistic patterns may reveal meaning without accepting a strong language-as-use theory.
charity.decisiveQualification: The evidential interpretation still depends on some account connecting patterns of use to semantic content.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dependence claim follows once empirical patterns require a semantic interpretation, although the exact strength of that presupposition is implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete external-pattern and grammar analogy is supplied, but competing semantic accounts are not comparatively assessed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports empirical-method calibration by identifying the semantic assumptions governing evidence from linguistic behavior.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly accommodates an external approach while preserving the narrower point that interpretation remains theory-dependent.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt discusses speech-pattern evidence, an analogy with approaches to grammar, and whether external patterns map onto speaker psychology.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: Historically diverse religious and philosophical traditions often disagreed about substantive norms while sharing an objective conception of value, providing a presumptive historical advantage for realism.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker directly addresses Lance and introduces C. S. Lewis's historical convergence case from an explicitly realist perspective.

response.rationale: This constructive historical case advances a central realist bridge by alleging cross-tradition convergence on objective value despite normative disagreement.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it presents a clear historical route and multiple examples, but compresses comparability and independence warrants.

precisionFindings.rationale: The convergence thesis is recoverable, but objective value spans ethics, aesthetics, and religion, and the relevant traditions are broadly grouped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited examples make convergence plausible, but broad historical probability exceeds the excerpt's limited comparative documentation.

charity.alternative: Shared normative language across traditions may not encode contemporary stance-independent moral realism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical convergence requires translation and category evidence connecting each tradition's claims to objective value in the relevant sense.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Convergence on objectively intended value would support a presumption, but the inference requires comparability, independence, and category-stability bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several traditions are named, but representative primary support, translation defenses, and serious rival interpretations are absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central realist historical-convergence bridge and thereby bears strongly on the claimed historical advantage.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move largely treats diverse traditions as sharing one category without resolving the strongest semantic and historical qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites Daoist, Jewish, Christian, Platonist, Aristotelian, and other traditions as sharing value objectivism despite disagreement.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Because contemporary metaethical categories are historically recent, projecting them backward risks anachronistically misclassifying earlier thinkers and cultures as realists or anti-realists.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer follows McAllister's direct question and develops Bush's characteristic skepticism about attributing determinate metaethical views.

components.text: Whether historically diverse claims can be classified as instances of the same contemporary realist metaethical category.

response.rationale: The reply expressly identifies backward projection of recent analytic categories as a defect in the historical-convergence inference while allowing some clear cases.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly diagnoses the classification premise and states the defeating consequence without claiming that all historical attribution is impossible.

precisionFindings.rationale: The risk of anachronistic category projection is clearly stated and expressly qualified by admitting some plausible historical cases.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asserts a risk rather than universal misclassification and supplies explicit counterexamples and caution.

charity.alternative: Some historical texts contain sufficiently explicit commitments to warrant realist classification.
charity.decisiveQualification: Local clear cases do not establish broad convergence across unlike traditions and vocabularies.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from recent category formation to caution about broad retrospective classification is valid and carefully qualified.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies category history and a concrete ancient example, though it does not document the dating and translation issues in detail.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the indispensable historical-attribution step needed for a broad realist convergence argument.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply expressly grants clear historical cases and confines its objection to unsupported broad projection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grants recognizable metaethical overtones in some ancient texts while warning against general backward projection of modern categories.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: Restricting historical evidence to recorded philosophical and intellectual systems still reveals broad convergence toward realist interpretations of value claims despite substantive normative disagreement.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker responds appreciatively to Lance, then reformulates Lewis's argument from the acknowledged realist side of the exchange.

components.text: Whether recorded philosophical and intellectual systems, rather than undifferentiated populations, exhibit comparable realist commitments.

response.rationale: The reply narrows the historical evidential demand to recorded systems with articulated value claims, preserving the convergence issue while avoiding attribution to entire populations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe is relevant and justified, but it does not fully answer the remaining translation and category-equivalence challenge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evidential population is narrowed, but 'every single' system and 'realist perspective' remain broad across heterogeneous traditions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The near-universal convergence language substantially outruns a list of traditions without primary documentation or rival interpretation.

charity.alternative: Recorded systems can use objective-sounding value language without expressing the same stance-independent metaethical thesis.
charity.decisiveQualification: Restriction to elite texts improves evidence quality but does not itself establish semantic equivalence across systems.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Narrowing the population improves the inference, but the step from articulated value claims to shared realism remains materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Numerous systems are listed, but no representative passages, translations, independence analysis, or alternative comparison are supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central historical-convergence bridge with a more defensible, recorded evidential population.

representationalCharity.rationale: The narrowing is fair, yet the argument continues to assume the decisive cross-tradition equivalence it must establish.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt lists Stoicism, Epicureanism, Hinduism, Daoism, and Confucianism as recorded systems apparently assuming realism about value.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Translation problems, non-equivalent normative vocabularies, and later cultural contact undermine confident claims that independent traditions converged historically on moral realism.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker answers the request to assess Lewis's evidence and reiterates Bush's thesis that ordinary people commonly lack metaethical views.

components.text: Whether the listed traditions use comparable normative vocabularies that warrant a common realist interpretation.
Whether apparent cross-tradition convergence is historically independent rather than shaped by later cultural contact.

response.rationale: The reply directly raises translation, lexical non-equivalence, and cultural-contact problems that bear on the decisive comparability and independence premises.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both decisive historical warrants, though it offers limited concrete historical demonstration within the selected span.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three limitations are separately identifiable and the conclusion is appropriately limited to undermining confident convergence claims.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker explicitly notes discomfort with specific examples and presents the considerations as limits on confidence.

charity.alternative: Specialist textual work might establish local equivalence and independent convergence for particular traditions.
charity.decisiveQualification: A set of local successes would still need representative breadth before supporting the universal or broad historical presumption.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Translation, lexicalization, and contact are independent defeaters of an unqualified inference from surface similarity to independent convergence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Relevant research and mechanisms are identified, but the speaker concedes limited command of concrete examples and supplies little direct documentation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central historical-convergence bridge at its comparability and independence requirements.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move allows case-specific research and directs attention to the evidential work needed rather than denying comparability in principle.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt discusses culture-dependent moral lexicons, cross-cultural lexicalization research, translation difficulty, and limits on specific examples.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: The distinction between agent and appraiser relativism may be structurally limited because a person can alternate between, and simultaneously occupy, the roles of acting and appraising.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker admits making the omission in his earlier realist teaching video and asks Lance to defend the distinction, identifying Derek McAllister.

components.text: Whether perspectival evaluation offers a conceptual route distinct from the preceding historical disagreement.

response.rationale: The move begins a new conceptual issue rather than answering the historical limitations; its material is issue-bearing but leaves the legal earlier target's decisive historical demand uncontacted.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is relevant to the broader debate's alternative-relativism route but does not answer the selected earlier historical challenge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The role-overlap claim is clear, but perspective shifts between epistemic standpoint, semantic index, and ontological ground.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Role overlap is established plausibly, but its alleged limitation on the semantic or ontological distinction needs a further bridge.

charity.alternative: One person can occupy both roles while the semantic standards associated with those roles remain distinct.
charity.decisiveQualification: Token-level role overlap does not by itself collapse the theories' different truth conditions or normative consequences.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Alternating or simultaneous roles do not alone entail that the theories are merely epistemically rather than ontologically different.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The first-person role example supports overlap, but no semantic analysis establishes the claimed theoretical collapse.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally advances the realist burden of showing that the agent-appraiser distinction collapses into one perspectival structure.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move focuses on overlapping persons and thereby underdevelops the strongest structural account of the distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that one person acts and appraises, characterizing the remaining difference as perspective and epistemic rather than ontological.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Agent relativism generates conflicting obligations when the standards of different agents or cultures authorize incompatible actions and demands.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted explanatory turn continues Bush's response and uses wallet-taking and cultural-intervention cases to expose conflicts.

components.text: Whether agent relativism has distinctive normative consequences despite a person's ability to occupy both agent and appraiser roles.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the collapse challenge by identifying conflicting obligations as a structural liability specifically generated by agent-relative standards.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It establishes a material consequence distinguishing the theories, though it does not yet fully specify appraiser relativism's contrasting semantics.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly confined to agent relativism and to cases where different standards authorize incompatible actions or demands.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stipulated incompatible standards, conflicting agent-relative obligations follow from the view as characterized.

charity.alternative: Agent relativism might specify priority or jurisdiction rules that resolve cross-agent conflicts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such rules would require additional structure not supplied by the simple individual- or culture-relative account under discussion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conflict follows coherently from incompatible agent-relative standards, with only the absence of priority rules limiting generality.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete individual and cultural conflict cases support the conceptual conclusion, though the selected excerpt only begins their development.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally helps distinguish the proposed anti-realist alternative from agent relativism by exposing the latter's normative conflict.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move targets the simple version and acknowledges that a more respectable version would need substantial further development.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt introduces individual-level agent relativism and signals concrete cases in which acting on different standards creates a challenge.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Appraiser relativism gives moral assertions perspective-indexed descriptive content without imposing the externally generated obligations associated with agent relativism.
moves.attributionBasis: Bush explicitly contrasts appraiser relativism with the conflict cases he has just developed for agent relativism.

components.text: Whether role overlap eliminates the semantic and normative distinction between agent and appraiser relativism.

response.rationale: The reply expressly identifies different semantic content and the absence of externally generated obligations as reasons role overlap does not collapse the theories.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts both the semantic and practical dimensions of the collapse claim and states the defeating contrast.

precisionFindings.rationale: Perspective-indexed assertion content and externally generated obligations are clearly separated as distinct theoretical dimensions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Under the definitions developed, appraiser relativism lacks the particular normative conflict attributed to agent relativism.

charity.alternative: Both theories remain perspectival even if their semantic clauses and practical consequences differ.
charity.decisiveQualification: Sharing a perspectival genus does not eliminate a substantive difference in truth conditions or obligations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction is explicit and directly shows why shared role occupancy does not imply semantic or normative identity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual contrast is supported by the preceding conflict analysis, though a fully formal semantic account is not given.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central burden of articulating a coherent appraiser-relative alternative distinct from agent relativism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the shared genus while explaining why the proposed collapse overlooks decisive semantic and normative differences.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts criticism of agent relativism's normative problem with appraiser relativism's perspective-indexed semantic thesis.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Appraiser relativism is a genuine metaethical position with semantic and metaphysical commitments, rather than merely a description of variation among moral practices.
moves.attributionBasis: Bush begins with an explicit clarification and distinguishes descriptive relativism from appraiser relativism's semantic and metaphysical theses.

components.text: Whether appraiser relativism is merely a description of changing perspectives rather than a genuine metaethical theory.

response.rationale: The reply identifies semantic and metaphysical commitments that persist even without interpersonal variation, defeating a purely descriptive interpretation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly isolates the decisive test and explains why appraiser relativism remains metaethical even in a one-person case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move precisely distinguishes descriptive variation from semantic and metaphysical commitments and supplies a clear limiting case.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stated semantic and metaphysical theses, classification as a metaethical position follows without evidential overreach.

charity.alternative: Appraiser relativism may still be explanatorily thin even if technically metaethical.
charity.decisiveQualification: Explanatory thinness does not reduce a semantic and metaphysical thesis to mere descriptive sociology.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The solitary-appraiser case cleanly separates the theory's semantic structure from actual variation and completes the classification inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual example and comparison with familiar metaethical classifications strongly support the claim, with little empirical dependence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly completes a major part of the anti-realist burden to articulate a genuinely metaethical alternative.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move answers the strongest classification objection while leaving open separate questions about explanatory value.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that appraiser relativism persists with one person and locates its content in moral semantics and metaphysical implications.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: Even when agent and appraiser relativism are both properly metaethical, they may remain forms of one underlying relativism differentiated chiefly by the perspective from which evaluation occurs.
moves.attributionBasis: McAllister explicitly clarifies his earlier wording and develops an extended perspectival analogy before asking whether his interpretation is correct.

components.text: Whether substantive semantic and normative differences prevent both theories from instantiating one underlying perspectival relativism.
Whether granting appraiser relativism genuine metaethical status defeats the claimed common underlying structure.
Whether different practical consequences demonstrate distinct underlying rather than merely species-level theories.

response.rationale: The reply grants metaethical status but argues that the remaining differences concern evaluative perspective, thereby directly pressing the common-genus claim against all three contrasts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive distinctions and makes a clear concessive argument, though it does not explain why shared genus erases species-level significance.

precisionFindings.rationale: The concessive thesis is recoverable, but 'perspective' remains unstable between semantic index, evaluator role, and epistemic access.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker marks the interpretation as provisional, but the claim of only one relevant difference exceeds the developed analysis.

charity.alternative: Theories can share a relativist genus while differing substantively in truth conditions, metaphysics, and obligations.
charity.decisiveQualification: A common perspectival feature establishes taxonomy, not theoretical collapse or equivalence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Shared perspectival structure supports common classification, but the inference to one underlying position needs a criterion of identity not supplied.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The perspectival analogy supports similarity, yet no semantic or metaphysical analysis shows the stated contrasts are theoretically unimportant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central realist burden of collapsing the proposed alternatives into one underlying relativism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges the semantic classification but gives insufficient weight to the strongest species-level differences already identified.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly grants proper metaethical classification while arguing that both positions are relativisms differentiated mainly by perspective.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: External cultural standards can bind an agent only as the agent understands those standards, so first-person epistemic mediation restores a structural similarity between agent and appraiser relativism.
moves.attributionBasis: McAllister acknowledges Bush's explanation and then introduces a distinct epistemic route to his continuing collapse argument.

components.text: Whether external standards create a practical distinction once an agent can act only through a first-person understanding of them.
Whether epistemic mediation bears on the claimed semantic or metaphysical distinction.
Whether externally generated conflicting obligations remain distinct despite the agent's mediated access.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the practical contrast by arguing that external standards reach the agent through first-person interpretation, but it does not contact the independent metaethical-status argument.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive practical component and one conflict component, while leaving the semantic-metaphysical classification component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The epistemic point is clear, though 'from his own perspective' risks sliding between access to a standard and the standard's source.

calibrationFindings.rationale: First-person mediation is plausible, but the claimed collapse requires more than the acknowledged epistemic access condition.

charity.alternative: An externally sourced standard can remain external even though an agent learns or interprets it fallibly.
charity.decisiveQualification: Epistemic mediation does not transform the truth-maker or normative source into the agent's own perspective.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference equivocates between first-person epistemic access and first-person grounding of obligation, so collapse does not follow.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The mediation premise is supported by an intelligible scenario, but the stronger structural conclusion lacks independent warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary realist bridge concerning how first-person interpretation bears on external standards.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move materially underweights the strongest distinction between access to a standard and the constitution of that standard.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that an agent is bound by other cultures' standards only as understood and treats that mediation as a route to collapse.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Epistemic mediation is not distinctive to agent relativism and does not make it false, because moral realist views face comparable limitations on access to relevant facts or standards.
moves.attributionBasis: Bush immediately rejects the proposed distinctive problem, compares realism's epistemic access, and warns against consequence-based rejection.

components.text: Whether first-person epistemic mediation uniquely undermines agent relativism or collapses it into appraiser relativism.
Whether shared access limitations establish identity of the underlying metaethical positions.

response.rationale: The reply expressly distinguishes an epistemic limitation from falsity or metaphysical identity and adds that comparable access problems arise for realist theories.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly identifies the access-to-truth inference as defective and states both the defeating consequence and a parity consideration.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reply clearly separates truth, epistemic access, and comparative distinctiveness, while expressly allowing realist exceptions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The parity claim is qualified because some realist views invoke acquaintance or self-evidence, and the core non sequitur is firmly supported.

charity.alternative: Some realist theories claim direct acquaintance or self-evident access and therefore avoid the parity problem.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even where parity fails, mediated access still does not establish that agent relativism is false or identical to appraiser relativism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between an epistemic problem and falsity or theoretical identity is explicit and defeats the central inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete realist access alternatives and the general parity comparison are supplied, though the range of realist theories is not exhaustive.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary anti-realist parity bridge by showing that mediation is neither uniquely damaging nor truth-determining.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply expressly grants the strongest realist exception while preserving the independent logical objection to the collapse inference.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares realist access problems, grants direct-acquaintance and self-evidence exceptions, and denies that mediation makes a view false.
